initial_observation.encounter_context: The patient was referred to the Emergency Department by a nephrologist with a diagnosis of acute kidney injury associated with a three-month history of symptoms.
initial_observation.chief_complaint: Progressive dyspnea on exertion, fatigue, rash, and weight loss.
initial_observation.first_contact_summary: He initially presented to his primary care physician with a cough. Chest X-ray was unremarkable and proton pump inhibitor prescribed with partial symptom improvement; gradually developed dyspnea on exertion, fatigue, and weight loss. Mild anemia, elevated CRP and rheumatoid factor were noted. History included resected malignant melanoma of the left foot. Cardiology referral found a systolic murmur and mild to moderate mitral regurgitation with leaflet prolapse. Rheumatology referral noted elevated ESR, increasing CRP and RF, and a new petechial rash; a skin biopsy showed suppurative folliculitis; prednisone prescribed with partial improvement but tapering was not tolerated. Pulmonary function testing showed mild restriction. Nephrology evaluation showed worsening proteinuria, microscopic hematuria, and elevated creatinine. On arrival to ED, the patient had hypertension, crackles at lung bases, grade III/VI apical systolic murmur radiating to left axilla, non-blanching petechiae on lower extremities and torso, acute kidney injury, microscopic hematuria, low C3 level. Initial diagnosis was rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis secondary to vasculitis; intravenous methylprednisolone treatment was begun and echocardiogram was planned for the following Monday.
known_prior_history: malignant melanoma of the left foot resected

evidence_items.source_text: On arrival in the Emergency Department, the patient continued to complain of dyspnea on exertion and fatigue. Review of systems was otherwise negative. The patient’s initial vital signs included a blood pressure of 155/75. He was afebrile and appeared comfortable. Cardiopulmonary examination was notable for crackles at both lung bases and a grade III/VI apical systolic murmur that radiated to the left axilla. Non-blanching petechiae were present over the bilateral lower extremities and torso.
Laboratory investigations showed mild anemia and elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) and rheumatoid factor (RF) (Table 1).

Repeat laboratory investigations showed worsening proteinuria and microscopic hematuria, and a newly elevated creatinine level of 3.20 mg/dL from a baseline of 0.89–1.02 mg/dL (Table 1), which prompted referral to the Emergency Department.

Given the findings of hypertension, acute kidney injury, microscopic hematuria, and a low C3 level, the patient was diagnosed with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, secondary to vasculitis, and treatment was begun with intravenous methylprednisolone 1000 mg daily.

However, the following morning, the medical team performed a cardiac point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) (Figures 1–3, Videos 1–3). Imaging showed that left ventricular systolic function appeared normal. However, the mitral valve had markedly thickened leaflets, prolapse, and moderate to severe mitral valve regurgitation. The left atrium was enlarged. The inferior vena cava was dilated with reduced respiratory variation. These findings raised the clinical suspicion for infective endocarditis and heart failure due to valvular insufficiency.

An urgent cardiology consultation was requested and a transthoracic echocardiogram was performed on the same day, which showed thickening of both mitral valve leaflets and a vegetation on the posterior leaflet.
Blood cultures were positive for Streptococcus mutans.
Treatment with intravenous ceftriaxone was commenced and steroids were rapidly tapered. Infectious disease and cardiothoracic surgery services were consulted.

Transesophageal echocardiography demonstrated mitral valve vegetations with rupture of the chordae tendinae. There was 4+ mitral regurgitation and 1–2+ aortic regurgitation, and a Lambl’s excrescence was seen on the aortic valve.

On hospital day 10, the patient developed an acute stroke involving the territory of the right middle cerebral artery, resulting in severe neurological deficit with a National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) score of 18 (moderate to severe stroke). A successful embolectomy was performed, resulting in a return to normal baseline function with an NIHSS score of 0. His antibiotic was switched to intravenous penicillin.

On hospital day 14, he underwent a successful bioprosthetic mitral valve replacement and debridement of a 5 mm excrescence on the aortic valve. Histopathology of the mitral valve demonstrated fibrosis, extensive acute and chronic inflammation, and necrosis. Gram’s stain showed numerous Gram-positive cocci in pairs and short chains. The aortic valve lesion that was initially interpreted as a Lambl’s excrescence also demonstrated necrosis, inflammation, and Gram-positive cocci.

On hospital day 25, he was discharged to an acute rehabilitation center with a plan to complete four weeks of intravenous penicillin from the date of surgery. His creatinine had decreased to 1.2 mg/dL.

accepted_aliases: infective endocarditis due to Streptococcus mutans
